canonical_topic: Withdrawal rate is limited by the storage/pipeline pressure differential
definition: When gas is withdrawn from storage, a compressor creates suction to draw gas out and push it into the pipeline; the speed of that withdrawal depends on the pressure differential between the storage facility and the pipeline.
core_idea: Once withdrawal reaches a perfect vacuum on the suction side, the pressure differential — and therefore the flow rate — stops increasing, so the storage facility's own pressure becomes the hard ceiling on how fast gas can be pulled out.
key_points: A compressor pulls gas from storage into the pipeline by suction.
Flow speed is a function of the pressure differential between storage and pipeline, not the compressor alone.
A perfect vacuum caps the achievable differential, making storage pressure the binding constraint on withdrawal speed.
relationships: Ties directly to the facility's maximum pressure constraint, which sets the upper bound on storage-side pressure and therefore withdrawal speed.
trading_implications: Deliverability (how fast gas can actually be withdrawn to meet demand spikes) is physically capped by facility pressure, which matters for valuing storage optionality during high-demand periods.
caveats: Assuming withdrawal rate scales only with compressor power rather than being capped by the storage-pipeline pressure differential.
